passage: The line to the school gate was loud, and the bus was due any minute. Mehak tugged Ms Sonali's sleeve. "There is a dinosaur in my house. He is green and he eats my cornflakes!" Her eyes were wide, and she half believed it herself. Ms Sonali smiled. "What a fun story! Is he real or pretend?" Mehak thought hard, scuffing her shoe. "Pretend," she said. "But maybe he hides when you come." "Then he is a very shy pretend dinosaur," said Ms Sonali. "Tell me more tomorrow." Mehak skipped to her bus.

qa.q: How does Mehak seem to feel about her dinosaur story?
qa.a: Mehak seems excited and half convinced, with wide eyes, and even after saying "Pretend" she adds that he might hide when the teacher comes.

qa.q: How did Ms Sonali respond well, and what would be harmful?
qa.a: She enjoyed the story and asked if it was real or pretend. Punishing the story as a lie would confuse imagination with deceit. 🙂

qa.q: How might Ms Sonali have felt hearing about the dinosaur?
qa.a: Ms Sonali was probably amused and interested, since she smiled, called it a fun story and asked Mehak to tell more tomorrow.

grounding: A child says she has a dinosaur at home, half believing it, and a teacher asks if it is real or pretend without punishing the imagination.

passage:
Note from Vidya's teacher, for home.
At circle time, Vidya told Sabina, "I have a real dinosaur at home. He sleeps under my bed and eats bananas." Sabina's eyes went round. Vidya looked very sure, even a little worried he might be hungry. I said, "What a fun story! Is it real or pretend?" Vidya thought hard. "Pretend... but a little bit real." Then the whole circle drew banana-eating dinosaurs. 🦕 You may hear more about him at dinner!

qa.q: What did Vidya say her dinosaur eats?
What does Vidya's worry about the dinosaur being hungry suggest?
qa.a: She half believed her own story; she felt playful and a little unsure where pretend ended and real began.

qa.q: Why was asking "real or pretend?" a wise choice?
qa.a: It enjoyed her imagination while gently helping her tell story from fact, without calling it a lie.

qa.q: How might Sabina see Vidya's dinosaur story?
qa.a: Sabina seems amazed and excited, with round eyes, and enjoys the story.

grounding: A young girl tells an imaginative story about a dinosaur at home, and a teacher enjoys it and asks whether it is real or pretend.

passage: At the village shop, Hemant leaned on the counter. "Yusuf Chacha, there's a dinosaur living in our cowshed. It's bigger than the buffalo." Yusuf Chacha raised his eyebrows. "A dinosaur! What colour?" "Green. With spikes." Hemant looked towards the cowshed as if checking. His mother frowned. "Hemant, don't tell lies." Hemant's face fell. Yusuf Chacha winked at him. "What a fun story. Is it real or pretend?" Hemant grinned. "Pretend. But it's a good one." "The best one I heard today," said Yusuf Chacha, and gave him a toffee.

qa.q: Where did Hemant say the dinosaur lived?
qa.a: He said it was in the cowshed.

qa.q: How did Hemant feel when his mother said "don't tell lies"?
qa.a: He felt hurt and confused, because to him it was a playful story, not a lie.

qa.q: What did Yusuf Chacha do differently from Hemant's mother?
qa.a: He enjoyed the story and asked whether it was real or pretend, so Hemant could say it was pretend without shame.

qa.q: Why might Hemant's mother react differently from Yusuf Chacha?
qa.a: She may worry that stories will turn into lying, so she treats it as deceit rather than imagination.

grounding: A young boy tells a pretend story about a dinosaur, and an adult enjoys it and asks if it is real or pretend instead of calling it a lie.
